message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to tell my sister that her beating breast cancer wasn't impressive or inspirational. Let me start by understanding the situation better. Three years ago, my older sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Within six months, her cancer was cleared. She had minor radiation and then hormone therapy afterward. She's 100% fine and healthy, no need for surgery. We all came together and supported her during that time. Now, the issue is that she hasn't stopped constantly reminding us about how she's a cancer survivor. She's made it her identity. She's plastered it all over social media. I don't mind it because I can choose to ignore it. But this holiday season, she was unbearable. My breaking point happened when my dad, who has been dealing with nerve problems, was telling us how physical therapy wasn't working for him and he will likely need surgery. My sister started bringing up her cancer story again. I snapped and told her that her surviving breast cancer wasn't impressive or inspirational, that it has a survival rate of 96%, and to stop making everything about her story. My sister walked out of the room. I thought my family would back me up, but instead, my parents backed up my sister. My dad didn't say anything but he was on my sister's side. I don't know, maybe what I said wasn't the nicest way, but I don't think I was wrong in what I said. So, is it right or wrong for me to say that? Let me think about this step by step. First, I need to understand why I said what I did. I was frustrated because my sister kept bringing up her cancer story, especially when my dad was talking about his own health issues. It felt like she was overshadowing his concerns. I also mentioned that breast cancer has a 96% survival rate, implying that her survival wasn't that remarkable. But is that fair? Just because a condition has a high survival rate doesn't mean the experience isn't difficult or that the person's strength isn't commendable. Also, making someone's identity out of their cancer experience might be a way for them to cope or find meaning. On the other hand, I was feeling ignored and frustrated because my dad's issues were being overshadowed. It's valid to feel that way, but the way I expressed it might have been hurtful. I also need to consider how my parents reacted. They backed my sister, which might indicate that they felt my comment was harsh or insensitive. That makes me think that maybe I could have expressed my feelings differently without dismissing her experience. Perhaps instead of saying her survival wasn't impressive, I could have expressed that I felt her bringing up her story overshadowed my dad's concerns. That way, I address the issue without attacking her personally. I also need to think about the impact of my words. Telling someone that their struggle wasn't impressive can be really hurtful, especially if they've been through something difficult. Even if the survival rate is high, the emotional and physical toll can still be significant. Moreover, making someone's identity out of their cancer experience might be a way for them to connect with others or find a sense of purpose. Dismissing that could make them feel invalidated. In the future, maybe I can find a more constructive way to express my feelings without attacking her. It's important to communicate my needs without making the other person feel diminished. So, in conclusion, while I can understand why I felt the need to speak up, the way I expressed it might have been hurtful and insensitive. It's important to address the issue without dismissing someone's experience.
